To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we report the first outbreak of HAdV A31 in stem cell transplant (SCT) recipients.

we describe a prolonged outbreak of human adenova A31 in allogenous stem cell transplant recipients, which was caused by a single source of infection and was associated with high morbidity and mortality.
we report a large outbreak of HAdV A31, which was transmitted from patient-to-patient via contaminated medical devices, and that the infection was associated with significant clinical consequences.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the outbreak of HAdV-A31 in allogenic stem cell transplant recipients; (2) the analysis of the outbreak and the routes of transmission; and (3) the medical consequences of the outbreak.
the development of new methods and materials for the production and processing of polyolefins.

the development and application of new methods of mathematical modeling of the dynamics of the epidemic process, the development of mathematical models for the study of the dynamics of epidemics, the study of the effectiveness of various measures to prevent the spread of infectious diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the outbreak was caused by the HAdV-A31 strain and that the outbreak was not associated with any other HAdV strains.
the HAdV-A31 outbreak was most likely caused by an infected healthcare worker (HCW) with an unrecognized HAdV-A7 infection.
HAdV A31 was the causative agent of a prolonged outbreak at CAST, and the outbreak was caused by a combination of transmission via environmental contamination and person-to-person spread.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HAdV A31 is not a rare virus in allogeneically stem cell transplant (SCT) recipients.
we have identified the source of the outbreak and the routes of transmission and that we have implemented a new strategy to reduce the incidence of infections in our patients.
HAdV-A31 is a serious pathogen for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell recipients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
adenovirus A can cause prolonged outbreaks in transplant recipients, and it may be difficult to identify the exact source of infection.
HAdV-A31 is associated with a severe clinical course, and that the virus can be transmitted by asymptomatic carriers.
HAdV-A31 is a pathogen with the potential to cause a serious infection among immunocompromised patients.
